evidence.claim: A wartime road promise became a coastal connection across Annette Island.
evidence.quote: In exchange, the US promised to build a road connecting the ocean-side city to Alaska's Inside Passage

evidence.claim: Walden Point Road follows the forest’s edge above the ocean for 14.7 miles between Annette Bay and Metlakatla.
evidence.quote: This byway has many breathtaking views as you travel the 14.7 miles of Walden Point Road from Annette Bay to the community of Metlakatla.

evidence.claim: Alaska’s scenic-byways program highlights its waterfalls, spawning creeks and offshore island views.
evidence.quote: Waterfalls are plentiful, and some beautiful creeks that support fish spawning.

evidence.claim: In clear weather, the views reach Gravina Island, Prince of Wales Island and the Percy Islands.
evidence.quote: it is possible to see Gravina Island, Prince of Wales Island, the Percy Islands and off across the vast ocean when the weather is clear.

evidence.claim: Pullouts provide places to stop along the route.
evidence.quote: Pullouts along the route provide ample opportunity to enjoy these sights

evidence.claim: follows the forest’s edge above the ocean
evidence.quote: The road travels along the edge of the forest and overlooks the ocean

evidence.claim: During World War II, the United States promised the Metlakatla Indian Community a road to the Inside Passage in exchange for permission to construct and operate a military airbase on Annette Island.
evidence.quote: During World War II, the United States made a treaty with the Metlakatla Indian Community to permit construction and operation of a military airbase on Annette Island. In exchange, the US promised to build a road connecting the ocean-side city to Alaska's Inside Passage

evidence.claim: The road was meant to allow year-round ferry service to Ketchikan.
evidence.quote: in order to allow year-round ferry service to Ketchikan

evidence.claim: Construction began in 1998, and Department of Defense crews completed the road early in 2010 through an innovative readiness training program.
evidence.quote: The work of building Walden Point Road began in 1998. The Department of Defense military completed Walden Point Road early in 2010 in an “innovative readiness training” program.

evidence.claim: It opened access to central parts of the island previously reached only by old logging roads.
evidence.quote: The completion of the road increases access to much of the central part of the island, previously only accessible through old logging roads.

evidence.claim: Start at Annette Bay, with views toward Ketchikan, and continue toward Metlakatla past the coastal landmarks of Walden Rocks and Japan Bay.
evidence.quote: Scenic views from Annette Bay to Ketchikan as well as other local landmarks and fishing spots such as China town, Walden Rocks, and Japan Bay.

evidence.claim: Closer to town, the view includes the Dall Islands at Gravina’s southern end and the peninsula occupied by the Metlakatla Indian Community.
evidence.quote: Closer to Metlakatla the views will include the Dall Islands at the south end of Gravina Island, Prince of Wales Island, the Percy Islands, the peninsula of Annette Island which is where the Metlakatla Indian Community resides.

evidence.claim: Downtown, the William Duncan Museum interprets the community’s migration and town history.
evidence.quote: the William Duncan Museum (to date the only building on the Historic Register of Historic Places) which is located downtown gives historical information about the migration and the town of Metlakatla.

evidence.claim: The drive begins at Annette Bay, with a view across the water toward Ketchikan.
evidence.quote: Scenic views from Annette Bay to Ketchikan

evidence.claim: From here, Walden Point Road continues to Metlakatla along the forest’s edge, overlooking the ocean.
evidence.quote: The road travels along the edge of the forest and overlooks the ocean

evidence.claim: The coastal landmarks along the journey include Walden Rocks and Japan Bay, with pullouts for stopping.
evidence.quote: other local landmarks and fishing spots such as China town, Walden Rocks, and Japan Bay. Pullouts along the route provide ample opportunity to enjoy these sights

evidence.claim: Clear weather makes the difference for the wider island panorama: Alaska’s byway description identifies Gravina Island, Prince of Wales Island and the Percy Islands as visible in those conditions.
evidence.quote: it is possible to see Gravina Island, Prince of Wales Island, the Percy Islands and off across the vast ocean when the weather is clear.

evidence.claim: Contact the Metlakatla Indian Community for visitor, fishing and hunting permits.
evidence.quote: Please contact MIC for your fishing, hunting, and visitor permits

evidence.claim: Four evenly spaced pilasters divide the shiplap front of the Father William Duncan House in Metlakatla.
evidence.quote: The front facade is faced in shiplap siding, with four evenly spaced pilasters.

evidence.claim: Tsimshian followers of William Duncan built the single-story wooden house in 1891.
evidence.quote: The single-story wood-frame structure was built in 1891 by the Tsimshian followers of the Anglican missionary William Duncan.

evidence.claim: It now houses the Duncan Cottage Museum.
evidence.quote: now hosting the Duncan Cottage Museum

evidence.claim: Decorative woodwork fills the shallow gable end, a small architectural detail on a house added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1972.
evidence.quote: There is decorative woodwork in the shallow-pitch gable end.

evidence.claim: added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1972.
evidence.quote: The house was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1972.

evidence.claim: Metlakatla’s longhouse has hand-carved totem poles and is used for Native dancing and ceremonies.
evidence.quote: the Metlakatla Longhouse has beautiful hand carved totem poles and is used for both Native dancing and ceremonies

evidence.claim: The community began here in 1887, when Tsimshian people migrated from British Columbia with missionary William Duncan.
evidence.quote: Annette Island Reserve (AIR) began in 1887 when a Tsimshian population migrated from British Columbia with their beloved spiritual leader missionary William Duncan to form what is now known as the Metlakatla Indian Community (MIC).

evidence.claim: They named their settlement after the Metlakatla they had left behind.
evidence.quote: They named the town New Metlakatla, after the town they had left behind, but later dropped the "New."

evidence.claim: The island received federal recognition as an Indian Reserve four years later, in 1891.
evidence.quote: In 1891, the island was officially recognized as a Federal Indian Reserve

evidence.claim: All land on the reserve remains in Metlakatla Indian Community ownership.
evidence.quote: All of the land on AIR remains in MIC ownership.

evidence.claim: Fishing, seaweed harvesting and hunting remain important to the community’s livelihood.
evidence.quote: Fishing, harvesting seaweed, and hunting are important to the tribe's livelihood.

evidence.claim: Along the road, waterfalls and creeks that support spawning fish are among the features highlighted by Alaska’s scenic-byways program.
evidence.quote: Waterfalls are plentiful, and some beautiful creeks that support fish spawning.

evidence.claim: The settlement followed a grid plan and included a church, school, cannery and sawmill.
evidence.quote: They laid out the town in a European-style grid pattern. It contained a church, a school, a cannery, and a sawmill.

flags: Road construction dates conflict: Alaska DOT gives 1998–early 2010; cache 01 and 07 describe work in 1997–2007. Used the state transportation source and omitted unsupported claims about present ferry frequency or improved mainland access.
Cache 02 dates the migration to 1891, while Alaska DOT and cache 01 give 1887 and distinguish reserve recognition in 1891. Used 1887. No tribal-authored history is supplied.

The cottage has limited standalone evidence; its moment is intentionally shorter than 90 words. The new cottage moment precedes the town-center moment by cached latitude; no street-by-street strip routing is supplied.

The current approximate 800-person canoe migration is supported in cache 08 but omitted in favor of the state account. No unsupported current factual claim otherwise identified. Permit note reflects the saved state page, not a live 2026 check.
